extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and critics of literature; creative writers interested in archetypal/symbolic criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Analytical framework for identifying and interpreting recurrent archetypal images, modes, and cyclical patterns in literature (apocalyptic/demonic/romantic/high- and low-mimetic). Useful for literary criticism and informed creative-writing that uses mythic symbolism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometrical and Architectural Imagery (the 'way')
rubrics_metrics.description: The human use of the inorganic world involves the highway or road as well as the city with its streets, and the metaphor of the 'way' is inseparable from all quest-literature; also belong geometrical and architectural images: the tower and the winding stairway, Jacob's ladder, the ascending spiral or cornucopia, the 'stately pleasure dome', the cross and quincunx patterns, the circle as the emblem of eternity, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing or composing quest/epic material, look for architectural/geometry motifs (roads, towers, ladders, spirals, circles, crosses) as metaphors of movement, ascent/descent, orientation or its loss. These images often index a narrative's relation to mythic/ritual passage or teleology. Examples: Dante's stairway, Yeats's tower, Kubla Khan's dome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apocalyptic vs Anagogic Relationship of Man and Nature
rubrics_metrics.description: On the archetypal level nature is the container of man. On the anagogic level, man is the container of nature, and his cities and gardens are no longer little hollowings on the surface of the earth, but the forms of a human universe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish levels: at an archetypal level nature frames humanity; at anagogic/spiritual levels human institutions embody or contain nature. Use this distinction to interpret whether an image emphasizes human appropriation/ordering of nature (city/garden) or nature's domination of human life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic Placement of Fire and Water Relative to Human Life
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic symbolism usually puts fire just above man's life in this world, and water just below it. Dante passed through a ring of fire and the river of Eden to go from purgatory to Paradise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat fire and light imagery as often connected to ascent, purification, and the angelic/divine realm; treat water imagery as linked to death, dissolution, the unconscious, or the underworld. Analyze narrative transitions through these elements as symbolic passages between existential or mythic levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fire as Purifying, Transmuting, and Heavenly Symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: Fire is associated with spiritual or angelic world: angels surrounded by light and fire, tongues of flame at Pentecost, the seraph's coal, Prometheus and Zeus's thunderbolt; in alchemy fire links to transmuting earth to gold and the purification of the human soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for fire-related motifs (halos, crowns, phoenix, burning tree, altar smoke) to indicate purification, divine presence, or transformative processes (both spiritual and alchemical). In creative use, fire can connote both heavenly radiance and the refining/transformative goal of the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Water Symbolism: Death, Chaos, and the Water of Life
rubrics_metrics.description: Water traditionally belongs to a realm below human life, the state of chaos or dissolution which follows ordinary death; yet apocalyptically we have the 'water of life' (fourfold river of Eden) and ritual forms like baptism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating water imagery, consider its ambivalence: as destructively chaotic (sea, drownedness) or as source of salvation/renewal (river of life, baptism, Ezekiel's fresh river). Context (apocalyptic vs demonic) determines whether water signals loss or regeneration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonic Imagery: Characteristics and Themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Opposed to apocalyptic symbolism is the world of the nightmare and the scapegoat, of bondage and pain and confusion; demonic imagery parodies and mocks the exuberant play of art by suggesting its imitation in 'real life'. It personifies vast, menacing, stupid powers of nature and the sense of inscrutable fate administered by remote invisible gods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify themes of parody, futility, sacrificial scapegoats (pharmakos), tyrant-leaders, and machinery of fate as markers of a demonic structure. Use examples (Dante's Inferno, modern dystopias like 1984) to anchor readings. In composition, use these elements to create a world of existential helplessness or ironic inversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonic Imagery across Domains (animal, vegetable, inorganic)
rubrics_metrics.description: The demonic animal world: monsters and beasts (wolf, tiger, vulture, serpent, dragon). The demonic vegetable world: sinister forests, wastelands, the tree of death, barren fig-tree, stake/gallows. The inorganic demonic world: deserts, rocks, ruins, perverted work, labyrinths, maelstroms, the ouroboros.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reading or creating, map domain-specific images to the demonic polarity: monstrous animals indicate predation/tyranny; hostile vegetation indicates danger, temptation, or decay; inorganic motifs (ruins, labyrinths, engines of torture) indicate perverted civilization and loss of humanizing work. These images often cluster to produce a pervasive sinister atmosphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogical Imagery and the Three Intermediate Modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Most imagery must deal with less extreme worlds than apocalyptic and demonic. Three intermediate structures correspond roughly to the romantic, high mimetic, and low mimetic modes; they produce 'atmosphere' by constellations of images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the tripartite intermediate scheme to situate imagery along a spectrum from idealized (romance) to realistic/commonplace (low mimetic). Determine which mode dominates to interpret how images function (idealizing, civilizing, or empirical).

rubrics_metrics.name: Romantic Mode — Analogy of Innocence
rubrics_metrics.description: Romance presents an idealized world where heroes are brave, heroines beautiful, villains villainous; organizing ideas are chastity and magic. Imagery includes parental/divine guardian figures, children, unicorns, pastoral sheep, the paradisal garden, fountains, purifying fire and elemental spirits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify pastoral, hortus_conclusus, guardian-spirit and purity motifs as signals of romantic/innocent structures. In composition, use these to evoke innocence, magical protection, ritual chastity, and an animistic world populated by benign spirits.

rubrics_metrics.name: High Mimetic Mode — Analogy of Nature and Reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizing ideas are love and form. Imagery emphasizes centripetal gaze, idealized human representatives (king, courtly mistress as goddess), proud/majestic animals (eagle, lion, peacock, swan), the capital city with court rituals, formal gardens and disciplined rivers like the Thames.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating imagery, associate formalized social/political symbols (royal sceptre, court structures, heraldic animals) with high mimetic mode. These images tend to idealize social order and fuse political/social authority with transcendent values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low Mimetic Mode — Analogy of Experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizing ideas are genesis and work. Images are ordinary experiences: farms, peasants, the modern metropolis (labyrinthine loneliness), animals like the ape and tiger as mimetic figures, the sea as destructive element, ironic/destructive fire, and emphasis on labour and empirical discovery of faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use low-mimetic markers (common situations, work, social realism, industrial imagery) to read literature grounded in ordinary experience. For creative-writing, employ these images to emphasize human labor, social parody, irony, and empirically-anchored spirituality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Displacement and Demonic Modulation (reversal of associations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonic modulation is the deliberate reversal of customary moral associations of archetypes: any symbol takes its meaning primarily from context. A serpent may be sinister in one tradition and innocent in another; romantic inversion includes sadism, Prometheanism, and diabolism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay attention to context-driven reversals: if a traditionally 'good' symbol is used malignly (or vice versa), this is a deliberate technique of displacement. In critique, identify whether reversal is ironic, satirical, redemptive, or subversive; in composition, use reversal to unsettle habitual associations and produce critical tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latent Archetypal Patterns as Critical Tools
rubrics_metrics.description: In pointing out the latent apocalyptic or demonic patterns in a literary work, we should not assume that this latent content is simply hypocritically disguised; it is one factor relevant to a full critical analysis and often lifts a work out of mere historicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat identification of latent archetypal structures as an essential analytic move. Use them to reveal deeper metaphorical cores of a text, but avoid reductive moralizing; latent patterns can coexist with overt meanings and provide critical insight into a work's mythic resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mythos / Cyclical Movement: Seven Cyclical Patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative involves movement from one structure to another; cyclical movement is the fundamental form of process. Seven cyclical patterns: (1) divine death-and-rebirth (sun/vegetation gods), (2) fire-world rhythms (daily sun, solstitial cycle, lunar three-day analogy), (3) human waking/dreaming and life/death cycles, (4) animal lives often cut off (nostos exceptions), (5) vegetable/seasonal cycle (dying and reviving vegetation gods), (6) civilizational organic cycle (growth, maturity, decline, nostalgia), (7) water cycle (rain → springs → rivers → sea/snow).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing narrative movement or composing mythic plots, map events to these cyclic patterns to detect or craft recurring motifs of death/rebirth, seasonal metaphor, solstitial symbolism, and water imagery. Use the four-phase schema (seasons/day/water-cycle/life-stages) to align symbolic time-frames across images.
